title: Why gravel bikes use flared drop bars
summary: See how drop-bar hand positions, flare, tire volume and geometry balance efficiency with control on mixed surfaces.

steps.title: Drop bars provide multiple useful hand positions.
steps.body: The tops, control hoods and drops each change hand location and body posture. That variety can reduce the need to hold one position throughout a long mixed-surface ride.
steps.keyFact: A drop bar is a posture and control system, not only an aerodynamic device.

steps.title: The lower drops widen outward.
steps.body: Flare places the hands farther apart in the drops than at the hood position. That can increase steering leverage and clearance when descending or controlling the bike on loose ground.
steps.keyFact: More flare is not automatically better; width, flare and reach are rider- and component-specific choices.

steps.title: Braking and shifting remain available from the primary riding position.
steps.body: Integrated controls keep brake and shift commands near the rider's hands. Exact lever ergonomics and actuation depend on the actual control/brake/drivetrain system.
steps.keyFact: Cockpit fit and control reach must work for the rider; bar shape alone does not guarantee good fit.

steps.title: Control comes from the whole bicycle.
steps.body: Flared bars contribute steering leverage, but tire grip, wheelbase, steering geometry, rider position and braking all influence mixed-surface control.
steps.keyFact: Bike handling should not be attributed to a single component in isolation.

challenge.prompt: What does handlebar flare primarily change?

options.label: The width/leverage of the lower drop position

challenge.explanation: Flare widens the lower drop position and changes hand placement/leverage.
